rv.q: Five stars is nowhere near enough for this heartfelt and hard-hitting treat of a show.
Writer Stephen Beresford’s musical adaptation of his own 2014 film is a triumph.
There’s hope and heartache, triumph and adversity, disco dancing and Welsh choirs — it’s the stuff of musical theatre heaven.

At this pivotal moment, the woman begins to sing the suffragette and Labour movement song, Bread and Rose, and gradually everyone joins in. It’s magnificently stirring – but the film-makers make a misstep. The singing is powerful not only because it’s traditional but because it’s grounded in reality.
This production drags her subtext kicking and screaming into the daylight.
The result is hugely charming and affecting, if imperfect.
Spirited feel-good musical relates a bittersweet true story of 1980s political activism
Samuel Barnett (never better) as the flamboyant actor Jonathan does a fine disco routine in the community hall.
For me, it just needs a bit — just a bit — more real drama at its heart to become the popular smash it wants to be.
It hasn't yet found the right sound or dramatic depth to do full justice to its subject matter.
Coming to London when many Reform councils across England have banned Pride celebrations, and with trans rights in danger under the current Labour Government, this musical is vital.
Pride feels on the brink of being the next big thing – and how glorious that the next big British musical is so proudly and fiercely queer and working class.

Among the other notable turns in an altogether terrific cast is diminutive scene stealer Gwen played by Gillian Elisa who can make answering a telephone funny and Samuel Barnett who manages a fourth wall-breaking, spotlight moment as un-dimmable Jonathan.
This wonderful new British musical does them justice.
The euphoria of the show’s conclusion, marking an event that really did change people and perceptions, is impossible to resist.
Pride is the show I have been waiting for in what is truly an impeccable piece of theatre.
To celebrate their story so vividly and joyously is a privilege.

Pride is about two communities coming together against the common enemy – and yes, there is one person in the valley who hates that and tries to ruin it. But there is also understanding, friendship, fun, and empowerment.
Instead, Matthew Warchus and Stephen Beresford, director and writer of the hit film respectively, have reunited to produce an utterly joyous and triumphant musical.
The final scene elicits one of the largest communal sobs I've ever heard in the theatre.
A fine balance between intense historical themes and heartwarming comedy, Pride is a well-crafted production that knows exactly when to move you and when to make you laugh.

cn.t: Critics overwhelmingly embrace this heartfelt musical adaptation, praising its balance of humor and emotion in telling the miners-LGSM story. Most find it triumphant and deeply moving, though a few cite dramatic shallowness.
